items.stem: A nurse must address a colleague’s hostile, publicly demeaning behaviour that is undermining teamwork and safety. Using TeamSTEPPS DESC guidance, which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Hold a timely private discussion using “I” statements and aim for a constructive win-win resolution
Confront the colleague loudly in front of the client so others witness accountability
Ignore the behaviour because interpersonal conflict never affects patient safety
Post a detailed complaint on social media before speaking with the colleague

rationales.A: Correct. AHRQ TeamSTEPPS DESC: choose a private location (not in front of patient/team), use “I” statements, time the discussion, and work toward a win-win solution for interpersonal conflict.
rationales.B: Incorrect. DESC advises a private location so parties can focus on resolving conflict rather than saving face; public confrontation can escalate harm.
rationales.C: Incorrect. DESC is indicated when hostile/harassing behaviours put patients or staff at risk of harm.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Social-media airing is not a TeamSTEPPS conflict-resolution method and breaches professionalism.

items.stem: During a sterile procedure, a nurse notices a colleague’s glove touch a nonsterile surface. Which TeamSTEPPS situation-monitoring action best describes speaking up to correct the break?

options.text: Cross-monitoring — watching each other’s back as a team safety net to catch errors early
Spying — covertly gathering evidence to punish the colleague later
Ignoring the break to avoid hurting the colleague’s feelings
Waiting until after patient harm occurs before discussing sterility

rationales.A: Correct. AHRQ: cross-monitoring means monitoring others’ actions, providing a safety net, and catching mistakes early (“watching each other’s back”); example includes calling out a break in sterile technique.
rationales.B: Incorrect. AHRQ explicitly states cross-monitoring is not spying.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Failing to interrupt an error misses the purpose of cross-monitoring as error prevention.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Cross-monitoring aims to correct issues before harm occurs.

items.stem: An Ontario nurse realizes recent untreated health issues are impairing concentration and may endanger clients. Which response best meets CNO Code of Conduct accountabilities?

options.text: Self-reflect, seek help, and do not practise while impaired by any substance or unsafe health state
Continue full independent practice while keeping the health issue secret from all supports
Use alcohol at work to steady nerves so clients are unaware
Ask a friend without nursing credentials to cover medication administration unsupervised

rationales.A: Correct. CNO Code 6.7–6.8: nurses self-reflect on health and seek help if health affects safe practice, and do not practise when impaired by any substance. OpenStax: impaired practice endangers clients; nurses must address impairment appropriately.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Secrecy without seeking help conflicts with the duty to seek help when health affects safe practice.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Practising while substance-impaired is expressly prohibited (CNO 6.8).
rationales.D: Incorrect. Unregulated coverage of nursing medication administration does not meet safe, competent care or accountability requirements.

items.stem: A client with contamination obsessions and washing compulsions begins evidence-based psychotherapy. Which treatment element is essential?

options.text: Gradual exposure to anxiety triggers while preventing the usual compulsive ritual (exposure and response prevention)
Encouraging longer and more frequent washing until anxiety disappears permanently
Arguing that the client’s obsessions are deliberately invented for attention
Withholding all explanation of treatment because insight never varies in OCD

rationales.A: Correct. Merck and OpenStax: CBT with exposure and response/ritual prevention gradually exposes the client to triggers while preventing rituals.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Increasing rituals reinforces the OCD cycle rather than preventing the compulsive response.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Obsessions are unwanted/intrusive; arguing or blaming is nontherapeutic.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Insight varies; education and collaborative ERP are standard.

items.stem: For a client with OCD starting exposure and response prevention, which nursing actions are indicated?

rows.text: Support gradual exposure to triggers while the client refrains from the usual compulsion
Teach relaxation techniques to help reduce anxiety
Mock the client’s obsessions as attention-seeking
Educate about prescribed SSRI therapy and monitor for side effects when ordered

rationales.R1: Indicated. ERP requires exposure with response prevention (Merck/OpenStax).
rationales.R2: Indicated. OpenStax nursing interventions include teaching relaxation techniques.
rationales.R3: Not indicated. Obsessions are unwanted; mocking is nontherapeutic and harmful.
rationales.R4: Indicated. SSRIs are pharmacologic treatment; nurses monitor/educate (Merck/OpenStax).

items.stem: A client who abruptly stopped long-term opioid use has yawning, lacrimation, rhinorrhea, mydriasis, and piloerection. Which interpretation is most accurate?

options.text: Findings fit opioid withdrawal; assess with a validated scale (e.g., COWS) and manage symptoms
Findings fit opioid overdose; the priority is that pupils are always pinpoint
Opioid withdrawal is usually immediately life-threatening like status epilepticus and needs deep sedation first
These autonomic signs only occur with alcohol withdrawal, never opioid withdrawal

rationales.A: Correct. Merck: mydriasis, piloerection, lacrimation/rhinorrhea, and yawning are specific opioid-withdrawal signs. OpenStax: use COWS/CINA and focus on symptom management in withdrawal.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Overdose triad includes pinpoint pupils and respiratory depression (OpenStax); mydriasis fits withdrawal more than typical overdose.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Merck: opioid withdrawal is distressingly symptomatic but not itself typically life-threatening.
rationales.D: Incorrect. These signs are described for opioid withdrawal (Merck).

items.stem: A client 24 hours after stopping heroin has anxiety, yawning, rhinorrhea, mydriasis, gooseflesh, and abdominal cramps. Complete the bowtie.

actions.text: Assess withdrawal severity with a validated scale (e.g., COWS) and provide ordered symptom-focused care
Administer high-dose naloxone repeatedly as the only intervention for these findings
Supportive monitoring and anticipate agonist/partial-agonist therapy (e.g., methadone or buprenorphine) per protocol
Encourage immediate unsupervised return to street opioid use to “self-treat”
Ignore autonomic signs because withdrawal never needs nursing assessment

parameters.text: Vital signs and withdrawal symptom trend
Pupil size only once at admission with no reassessment
Whether the client can leave without any safety or follow-up plan
Response to ordered medications for withdrawal symptoms

rationales.K1: Incorrect. Overdose features respiratory depression/pinpoint pupils; this vignette matches withdrawal.
rationales.K2: Correct. Yawning, rhinorrhea, mydriasis, piloerection, cramps fit opioid withdrawal (Merck).
rationales.K3: Incorrect. Serotonin syndrome is a different toxidrome not supported by this cue set.
rationales.K4: Incorrect. Hypoglycemia alone does not explain this autonomic cluster.
rationales.A1: Correct. OpenStax: assess with COWS and manage symptoms.
rationales.A2: Incorrect. Naloxone is for overdose/respiratory depression, not first-line for this withdrawal picture.
rationales.A3: Correct. Merck: substitution with methadone or buprenorphine plus supportive care.
rationales.A4: Incorrect. Unsupervised return to use is unsafe and not treatment.
rationales.A5: Incorrect. Withdrawal requires assessment and supportive management.
rationales.P1: Correct. Trend vital signs and withdrawal symptoms to guide care.
rationales.P2: Incorrect. Although GI comfort matters, the keyed monitoring priorities here are vital/withdrawal trends and medication response.
rationales.P3: Incorrect. Single unchecked pupil assessment is inadequate monitoring.
rationales.P4: Incorrect. Discharge without plan is unsafe.
rationales.P5: Correct. Monitor response to ordered withdrawal medications.

items.stem: Which teaching point is most important for preventing diabetic foot complications?

options.text: Examine the feet daily and wear properly fitting footwear; do not walk barefoot
Ignore small cuts because neuropathy means injuries cannot become infected
Soak feet in the hottest water tolerable without testing temperature first
Apply moisturizing lotion heavily between the toes every hour

rationales.A: Correct. Diabetes Canada: examine feet daily and wear properly fitting footwear. Merck: inspect daily; avoid walking barefoot; well-fitting shoes.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Diabetes Canada: unnoticed injuries can become infected and lead to serious complications.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Diabetes Canada: test bath water with the hand first because neuropathy may blunt heat sensation.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Diabetes Canada: moisturize if dry but not between the toes (maceration/infection risk).

items.stem: A community nurse teaches home fire safety. Which instruction about smoke alarms is best?

options.text: Test smoke alarms every month and replace units that are more than 10 years old
Testing once every 10 years is sufficient if the alarm looks clean
Smoke alarms are unnecessary if the home has a fire extinguisher
Never place alarms near bedrooms because nighttime waking is harmful

rationales.A: Correct. Health Canada and NFPA: test monthly; replace alarms more than 10 years old.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Monthly testing is required; a 10-year interval is for replacement, not testing.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Smoke alarms provide early warning and are not replaced by extinguishers alone.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Install alarms in/near bedrooms and on every level, including basement.

items.stem: Which home smoke-alarm actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Install alarms in bedrooms, outside sleeping areas, and on every level including the basement
Test alarms monthly using the test button
Replace alarms that fail testing or are more than 10 years old
Disable alarms permanently after one nuisance alarm from cooking
Create and practise a home fire escape plan

rationales.A: Correct. Health Canada/NFPA placement guidance for bedrooms, hallways/outside sleeping areas, every level including basement.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Do not permanently disable alarms; investigate false alarms and keep working devices (Health Canada).
rationales.E: Correct. Both advise having/practising an escape plan alongside working alarms.

items.stem: Complete the TeamSTEPPS DESC mnemonic used for conflict resolution.

B4.text: Cancel the conversation mid-sentence without closure

rationales.B1a: Correct. D — Describe the specific situation.
rationales.B1c: Incorrect. DESC includes timely discussion, not endless delay.
rationales.B1d: Incorrect. Clients are not blamed as the Describe step.
rationales.B2a: Correct. E — Express concerns about the action.
rationales.B2c: Incorrect. Public shaming is contrary to DESC.
rationales.B2d: Incorrect. Safety concerns must be addressed.
rationales.B3d: Incorrect. Suggest alternatives before punitive framing.
rationales.B4a: Correct. C — Consequences should be stated.
rationales.B4b: Incorrect. Consequences are stated, not concealed.
rationales.B4c: Incorrect. Focus on what is right, not who wins.
rationales.B4d: Incorrect. DESC aims for constructive closure.
